Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-02

Duration: ~78 minutes (scheduled)
Location: Zoom
Recording: enabled
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (Redwood Solutions Eng); Carlos Mendez (Vela CTO), Anika Bose (ML Platform), Ravi Patel (SRE), Mei Lin (Security), Jared (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, terse):
- Objective: plan a pilot for tenant-aware prefetching and quantized model serving in a VPC/private deployment, align on hit-rate targets and safety controls.
- Key asks: benchmark prefetch vs on-demand for KV cache, define cache key scheme to avoid leakage, agreement on pilot SLA & pricing, security docs.

Topics: pilot scope, KV-prefetch strategy, prefix vs full prompt keys, tenant isolation, eviction policy, cache key entropy, quantization impact on hallucination, batching configuration, VPC/on-prem networking, SOC2/KMS questions.

[00:00:00] Maya Chen: "Alright everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, real quick — we wanted to use this time to concretely scope a pilot that tests tenant-aware prefetching and quantized serving inside your VPC. So I'll hand it to Carlos to open with goals and then Liam will go through our proposed approach."

[00:00:22] Carlos Mendez: "Thanks Maya. So our main thing is we want to reduce per-token cost for our multi-tenant assistant while preserving tail latency at 95th p95 under 350ms. We're using a mix of short prompts and long context follow-ups. Key concerns: no leakage across tenants, and certs/compliance — Mei is on the call for that."

[00:00:41] Mei Lin: "Yep, security wise we need KMS integration, audit logs for cache reads/writes, and clear key rotation. SOC2 is a must. Also, Vela keeps some customer transcripts overnight for analytics — needs to be configurable."

[00:01:05] Liam Ortiz: "Cool. High level: Redwood runtime supports a KV prefix cache and an adaptive prefetcher. We'll test three modes: on-demand (no prefetch), conservative prefetch (hotset only), and aggressive prefetch (predictive looking ahead). Each mode has tradeoffs in memory and possibly stale prefix reuse. We'll also exercise 4-bit quantized model variants to measure inference throughput gains vs any small delta in output quality."

[00:01:34] Anika Bose: "When you say prefix cache, do you mean full prompt hashes or windowed prefix signatures? We've seen collisions before when using naive hashes at Vela." 

[00:01:46] Priya Desai: "Great question. Our recommended approach is a composite key: tenant_id + model_version + prefix_signature. The prefix_signature isn't just a naive SHA of entire prompt; we canonicalize, normalize whitespace, and include a short rolling signature over last N tokens to reduce collision surface. It's a balance between key entropy and index size. We can sample to estimate false-positive collisions."

[00:02:16] Ravi Patel: "Okay, but composite keys mean larger index footprint. We're memory-constrained on the private deployment nodes. How are you mitigating that?"

[00:02:29] Liam Ortiz: "We suggest a two-tiered index: an in-RAM LRU hotset for the top ~5-10% of keys by access frequency, backed by a compact persistent index for warm entries. Prefetch policy only loads to RAM hotset when predicted hotness crosses threshold. That keeps memory down but still gets most p95 wins."

[00:02:48] [crosstalk] Carlos: "...how do you measure hotness?"

[00:02:52] Priya Desai: "We run a light-weight synoptic sampler — 1% of requests are used to update a probabilistic frequency sketch (Count-Min or HyperLogLog variant) and we apply TTL decay. We can tune the sampling rate for Vela during pilot."

[00:03:18] Jared (PM): "What's the expected hit-rate lift with conservative prefetch? Give us a ballpark, like 10/20/30%?"

[00:03:24] Liam Ortiz: "Conservative prefetch typically nets a 12-25% effective token hit-rate increase depending on workload. Aggressive can push 30-50% but at higher memory/cost and risk of retrieving stale prefixes if prompts shift. We'll need your prompt corpus to estimate precisely."

[00:03:51] Anika: "We can provide a 10k prompt sample from our last two weeks of traffic, anonymized. Does Redwood need exact tokens for benchmarking?"

[00:04:00] Maya Chen: "Yes, for bench accuracy we prefer a representative corpus. You can either share hashed/anonymized versions or run the benchmarking harness inside your VPC and share metrics — whatever fits your security policies."

[00:04:18] Mei Lin: "We'd rather run inside the VPC. Sharing raw tokens outbound is a no-go. Is there a self-run harness?"

[00:04:25] Priya Desai: "We have a small benchmarking container and scripts that you can run on-prem or in your VPC to capture the same metrics. It emits CSVs and perf traces and doesn't leave your network unless you opt in. We'll share the repo link in the follow-up."

[00:04:42] Carlos: "Perfect. Now, on quantization, we've seen 4-bit models introduce occasional syntax glitches. How do you validate output quality?"

[00:04:52] Liam Ortiz: "We run automated eval suites and human spot-checks. For this pilot we'll compare full-fp16 baseline vs 4-bit and 6-bit quantized variants across your eval prompts. We'll flag any regression in intent, toxicity, or hallucination. Small regressions often happen in nuanced tasks, so we recommend a canary rollout for quantized models — traffic split and automatic rollback on metric drift."

[00:05:20] Maya Chen: "Also to note: the runtime can automatically route high-risk prompts to FP16 while using quantized models for the rest based on a policy. That's a common hybrid pattern for cost-sensitive customers."

[00:05:34] Ravi Patel: "Latency — we need p95 \u003c=350ms. Does prefetching affect tail latency?"

[00:05:41] Liam Ortiz: "Prefetching reduces generation latency for cache-hit prefixes. However prefetching itself introduces background I/O. We ensure that prefetch ops are bounded and low-priority so they don't steal CPU on the serving path. In practice, p95 drops with hit-rate increases; the challenge is handling cold starts and model-loading spikes, which we mitigate with warm-up and pre-warming policies."

[00:06:05] Carlos: "What about multi-tenant safety: if two tenants have overlapping prefix signatures, what prevents leak?"

[00:06:12] Priya Desai: "Tenant_id is the primary namespace separator: cache keys are always namespaced. In shared caches we enforce strict RBAC and encryption at rest, and we sign keys with tenant-scoped HMAC so that keys can't be forged or shared. We'll show the key derivation in the runbook. Also we recommend periodic key rotation to limit blast radius if a key is compromised."

[00:06:37] Mei Lin: "You mentioned audit logs earlier. Are cache reads/writes logged to an append-only audit trail? How heavy is that on storage?"

[00:06:45] Liam Ortiz: "Yes, we can emit read/write events to your existing logging sink (Kafka, S3, whatever). We support sampled logging to control storage — for full audit compliance you can enable 100% retention for a limited window. Events are lightweight JSON lines. For VPC we can push directly to your Kinesis/S3."

[00:07:07] Anika: "If we enable sampled audit logs at 5%, will that bias our hit-rate analysis?"

[00:07:12] Priya Desai: "You'd need aligned sampling across metrics; it's fine for gross perf measures, but for fine-grained correctness debugging we'd want 100% for the short pilot windows."

[00:07:26] [00:07:30] — Short audio interruption — reconnecting —

[00:07:54] Maya Chen: "Looping back, let's outline the pilot phases: 1) instrumentation & corpus selection (you run Redwood bench inside VPC or provide anonymized corpus) 2) small-scale prefetch experiments (hotset conservative) 3) quantized model canary and hybrid routing 4) production pilot with Dedicated nodes — roughly 4 weeks if all goes well."

[00:08:18] Carlos: "Timeline sounds good. We want to understand cost. Maya, can you share a sample cost calc: tokens saved vs additional Dedicated node cost?"

[00:08:27] Maya Chen: "Yes. We'll produce a cost model during the bench step. We'll show expected token-savings at different hit-rate curves and map to Dedicated commit tiers. I will send a spreadsheet with scenarios — that's one of the follow-ups."

[00:08:42] Ravi Patel: "Networking: we have strict egress rules. For on-prem test, can Redwood components run as containers that we deploy?"

[00:08:50] Priya Desai: "Absolutely. Our Private offering supports a customer-run control plane and inference nodes as containers. For the bench we can provide OCI images and Helm charts. For fully air-gapped setups, we have an offline bundle. We'll coordinate with your infra team for registry access."

[00:09:08] Mei Lin: "On KMS, we use AWS KMS with custom key policies. Is Redwood able to integrate with our CMKs?"

[00:09:13] Liam Ortiz: "Yes, we support BYOK via KMS/HSM. Keys are used for encrypting persisted cache entries and for signing key IDs. Access logs to KMS are retained in CloudTrail — we can cross-check."

[00:09:27] Anika: "What about eviction policy for the KV store? LRU can be unfair with bursty tenants."

[00:09:33] Priya Desai: "We support a few eviction strategies: global LRU, tenant-weighted LRU, and time-windowed TTL eviction. For multi-tenant fairness we generally recommend tenant-weighted policies where each tenant has a soft cap and we evict proportionally. That prevents noisy neighbors from starving others."

[00:09:51] Carlos: "Will tenant-weighted eviction increase bookkeeping complexity?"

[00:09:55] Liam Ortiz: "Slightly. It needs per-tenant counters, but it's still lightweight and can be approximated via sketches. We'll outline config knobs and tradeoffs in the runbook."

[00:10:08] Maya Chen: "Now — a bit of a pedantic but important thing — cache key canonicalization: whitespace, punctuation, metadata. How aggressive is Redwood about normalizing?"

[00:10:18] Priya Desai: "We canonicalize by trimming, lowercasing when configured, removing timestamps and ephemeral IDs using regex rules you can supply. We also support label-stripping for known structured fields. But we keep canonicalization configurable because some customers need case-sensitivity for domain-specific tokens."

[00:10:37] Ravi Patel: "Edge case: dynamic system prompts that inject tenant-specific tokens. How do we avoid these poisoning the cache?"

[00:10:44] Liam Ortiz: "We recommend separating system prompt layer from user prompt keying: i.e., hash system prompt separately and include system prompt version in the composite key. If system prompt changes frequently, set it to bypass cache or use a short TTL to avoid cross-temporal contamination."

[00:10:59] Anika: "Can we audit for accidental leakage? Like detecting identical completions served to different tenant IDs?"

[00:11:06] Priya Desai: "Yes, we can run a synthetic detection job post-hoc that looks for overlapping completion text across tenant namespaces and surface anomalies. It's something we include in the safety checklist for pilots."

[00:11:20] [00:11:30] Jared: "How invasive is key rotation operationally? Will it cause cache churn and perf regressions?"

[00:11:35] Liam Ortiz: "Rotation is designed to be staggered: generate new signing keys, start signing new cache entries while allowing old keys to expire gracefully. There is transient churn for entries that get re-generated, but that's manageable if you stage rotations during low traffic windows. We'll include a rotation playbook."

[00:11:52] Carlos: "Okay, let's talk metrics we'll collect during bench: p50/p95/p99 latency, token-per-second, cache hit-rate (by prefix length), memory footprint, model quality regressions, and tail error rates. Anything else?"

[00:12:04] Maya Chen: "Also CPU/GPU utilization, KV read latency, and auditing events per second. We'll create a dashboard template and share it."

[00:12:13] Mei Lin: "From security side: include MD5/hash of datasets and a proof that the bench harness doesn't exfiltrate data. We'll need an attestation doc."

[00:12:22] Priya Desai: "Understood — we'll include an attestation and the bench container is open-source so you can audit it yourself."

[00:12:35] Anika: "One more — batch sizing. For our interactive flows, what's the recommended batching window to preserve latency?"

[00:12:41] Liam Ortiz: "For interactive, we recommend micro-batches (e.g., 2-8 requests aggregated up to a 5-10ms window). Our runtime does continuous batching, so it opportunistically groups tokens across inflight requests while respecting per-request latency SLOs. The pilot will test a few batch window knobs."

[00:12:58] Carlos: "Any gotchas with quantization + KV cache? If the model outputs differ slightly, does that affect cache hit rates?"

[00:13:06] Priya Desai: "Yes. If quantized variants produce even small token differences on the prefix, those will be treated as cache misses. To mitigate, we recommend routing generation to the model family that was used to populate the cache or using normalization/hashing at an earlier step. We also support model-version-aware keys to avoid cross-model false hits."

[00:13:29] Maya Chen: "Round-up: immediate deliverables from Redwood are — bench harness repo, pricing spreadsheet, runbook for keying/isolation, and a draft pilot plan. Anything else the team wants from us?"

[00:13:42] Carlos: "Add the audit attestation and the bench container SHA. Also, can we get an example of tenant-weighted eviction in config form?"

[00:13:49] Priya Desai: "Yes, we'll include a sample Helm values snippet and a small simulator that demonstrates eviction behavior under bursty loads."

[00:13:59] Mei Lin: "And we'll need SOC2 + data flow diagrams for the VPC deployment — please include network ports, data sinks, and key management flow."

[00:14:09] Maya Chen: "Got it. We'll email a package.
Thanks everyone — final thing: schedule the 2-hour benchmark session for the week of April 13th. I'll put a doodle in. Anything else before we close?"
